title: Anonymous Prolegomena to Platonic Philosophy, in English
about: Translated for the Workshop from Hermann's Greek as the OCR gives it (Platonis Dialogi vol. VI, 1887, pp. 196-222), page by page, because no public-domain English translation exists (Westerink's of 1962 is in copyright). Where the scan is unreadable or the printed text is plainly corrupt the English says so in square brackets rather than guess; '[as printed]' marks a statement translated as the Greek has it although it may be a slip of the author or the printer. Chapter numbers are Hermann's. A page that begins or ends in mid-sentence begins or ends with '…'. Check it against the Greek beside it.

sections.english: PROLEGOMENA to the philosophy of Plato. 1. Aristotle, at the beginning of his theological philosophy [the Metaphysics], said that all men desire to know, and gave as proof of this our love of the senses: for we love the senses for this reason, that through them we may know something. I for my part would say that the philosophy of Plato has had the same fortune: for one may see all men wishing to draw from it, as from a spring, as much as each thinks useful to him. By 'all' I mean those at least who are in their natural state, who are not hardened, and who are not like bats, unable to face the light of the sun, those who think that only the things of sense exist and give no thought to the things of the intellect. And we would admire his philosophy still more if we set out both the history of the man and the character of his philosophy. Plato, then, the great, was the son of Ariston, son of Aristocles, on his father's side, and on his mother's side of Perictione, a descendant of Solon the lawgiver; and for this reason, in imitation of Solon, he set out the Republic and the Laws. He himself was called Aristocles, after his grandfather on his father's side, but his name was changed to Plato, either because of the breadth (platy) of his chest, or because of the width of his forehead, or (and this is the truth) because of the breadth and openness of his style. In the same way Theophrastus, who was formerly called Tyrtamus, had his name changed to Theophrastus because of the divine quality (theion) of his style. Plato was divine and Apollonian. That he was divine is clear both from himself and from dreams: from himself, because he called himself a fellow-servant of the swans [Phaedo 85b]; from dreams, in this way. Socrates his teacher, the day before Plato was to come to him, saw in a dream that a swan without feathers came into his lap, then grew its feathers and flew up, crying out something great and clear, so as to captivate all who heard it. This showed that …

… Plato would come to him unformed, but would become complete, and would so excel in his doctrines that all would long to hear them and none would be able, or would even try, to oppose them. And Plato himself, when he was about to die, saw himself become a swan and leap from tree to tree, giving much trouble to the bird-catchers, who could not catch him. Hearing this dream, Simmias the Socratic said that all men would strive to grasp Plato's thought, but none would be able to; each would make his interpretation according to what seemed right to him, whether he chose to read it as theology, or as natural philosophy, or in some other way. For both of them, Homer and Plato, have had the same fortune: because of the harmony of their style they are accessible to every reader, in whatever way one wishes to approach them. Not only do these dreams show that he was Apollonian, but so does the character of his life, which was purificatory; for such is the god too, as his very name shows: 'Apollo' means 'the one apart from the many' (a-pollōn), for the 'a' is a privative particle. Further, we infer that he was Apollonian from the time of his birth: he was born on the seventh of the month Thargelion, on which the Delians hold the festival of Apollo; and on the sixth of this month Socrates was born, on which they held the birthday festival of Artemis. This shows [a word here is unreadable in the scan] in Socrates, both in time and in reason. To give a complete account of his history, let us proceed by division. Everything that comes to be comes to be in a time and in a place; so Plato too, as one who came to be, was born at some time and in a place. Let us learn each of these, and also what happened at his birth and around it. As to time, he was born in the 88th Olympiad, in the archonship of Ameinias, while Pericles was still alive and the Peloponnesian wars were still being fought, six years younger than Isocrates; as to place, he was born in Aegina, his father Ariston having been sent at that time to Aegina by the Athenians as a settler. So much for the time and the place in which he was born. Around his birth, while his mother was still carrying him, his father saw this dream: that he should not lie with her until she had given birth. This signified that not for …

… pleasure should intercourse be chosen, but for the begetting of children alone, and that the child to be born should be born pure, taking no stain from intercourse during the pregnancy, which is shameful. Moreover his mother, after the birth, took him up Mount Hymettus, wishing to sacrifice to Apollo the Shepherd and to the Nymphs; she laid him down there, and on her return found his mouth filled with honey: for bees had come and done this, foretelling that the words that would flow from him would be sweeter than honey, as the poet says [Iliad 1.249]. He kept a diet not of animals but of plants. When he came of age he went to school with Dionysius the schoolmaster, whom he mentions in his Lovers; for he did not think it right to leave his own teacher unremembered. He studied with Ariston the trainer, for he took great care of this too, so that he won two contests, at Olympia and at Nemea. After these he studied also with Draco the musician [the scan reads 'Iphakonti'], who came from the school of Damon [some words here are bracketed by Hermann and garbled in the scan], the Damon whom he mentions in the Theaetetus [as printed]. He passed through these three, letters, gymnastics and music, so that he could urge his own pupils to be led through the same; for he knew that these three branches of education can set right the threefold soul: through letters he made exact its reasoning part, through music he tamed its spirited part, as through gymnastics he strengthened its desiring part. 3. After these he studied with the dithyrambic poets, wishing to benefit from their manner; indeed his first writing, the Phaedrus, is dithyrambic. He studied also with the tragic poets, wishing to draw their solemnity from them; and with the comic poets, wishing to benefit from their diction. Indeed he modelled himself on the manner of Aristophanes, who excels the other comic poets; and that he approved of his diction is shown by the epigram he wrote on Aristophanes, which runs: 'The Graces, seeking to take some sanctuary they wished to find, found the soul of Aristophanes.' He also emulated Sophron the writer of mimes, wishing to master imitation; for one who writes dialogues brings in an imitation …

… of characters. He studied also with painters, wishing to learn the varied mixing of colours; and so in the Timaeus he gives a long account of colours. All this he did until he was twenty. After this he went to Socrates and spent ten years with him, wishing to learn ethical philosophy. Finding that Socrates surpassed the rest, they say, he was about to give what he had worked at before to the fire, and spoke this verse: 'Hephaestus, come here: Plato has need of you now' [after Iliad 18.392]. He was seen to be as devoted to Socrates as anyone; indeed, when Socrates was on trial and in the court, he went up to the platform and burst out with these words: 'Though I am young, men of Athens, I have come up to the platform …'; but the jurors, angered, made him come down; and he left the court in grief, unable to bear staying there. After he had profited from Socrates in ethics, and had given Socrates himself trouble in their conversations, he set out writings, which came into Socrates' hands while he was still alive. For he had written the dialogue Lysis; and Socrates, having read it, said to his companions: 'This young man leads me where he likes, as far as he likes, and to whom he likes.' 4. After his time with Socrates he went off to the Pythagoreans, wishing to master from them the signifying of things through numbers; and so he mentions them often in the Timaeus. He studied also with Cratylus the Heraclitean and with Hermippus [as printed] the Parmenidean, wishing to learn the doctrines of Heraclitus and of Parmenides; and so two dialogues were written by him, the Cratylus and the Parmenides, in which he mentions the doctrines of these men. Having learnt that the Pythagoreans took the beginning of their philosophy from Egypt, he went to Egypt too, and having mastered geometry and the priestly art there he came back. Then he went to Phoenicia, met Persians there, and learnt from them the teaching of Zoroaster. From there he came to Sicily, wishing to see the craters of Etna; it was then too that he had his meeting with Dionysius. After this he came to Athens and set up a school near the lodging of Timon the misanthrope; and Timon, who was ill-disposed to everyone, as even the …

… epigrams on his tomb show, bore Plato's company very kindly. The epigrams are these: 'Here I lie, having broken off a wretched life; who I am you shall not learn; may you, wicked as you are, perish wickedly.' The second is this: 'Pass by this stone, neither bidding me farewell, nor asking who I am, nor whose son.' Part of his school Plato dedicated as a sanctuary to the Muses. Not only men studied with him but women too, Axiothea of Phlius and Lastheneia of Arcadia [the scan reads 'Zexytheia' and 'Aosthenia']. 5. This man was divine, as has often been said, and he was the discoverer of many things in life: of names, of things, and of a form of writing. Of names, the word 'quality' (poiotēs): it was not known before him. Indeed in the Theaetetus he says to Theodorus, making Socrates speak: 'perhaps "quality" will seem to you a strange and unaccustomed word' [Theaetetus 182a]. Aristotle shows it too, when he says in the Categories: 'by quality I mean …', saying 'I mean' because of the man who had coined the word; for if it had been in ordinary use he would surely have said not 'I mean' but 'is meant'; for he and all the ancients are accustomed to do this. He found also the name 'antipodes' and that of the 'oblong number'. He discovered things in natural philosophy, ethics, theology and politics. In natural philosophy, he showed that the magnet does not draw the iron, but that it is the air that pushes the iron towards it. In mathematics he discovered the so-called mean proportional, about which we spoke in the Apodeictic. For when the Athenians were struck by plague, they sent to Delphi to ask what they should do to be rid of it; and the god answered that they should double the altar and sacrifice so. The altar happened to be a cube, and they built another cube on top of it, thinking this was what the oracle meant; and since they were not rid of the plague by doing so, they went to Plato and asked him what they should do. He said: 'The god is reproaching you for your ignorance of geometry'; for the god was showing them not to think of the double in a layman's way, but to find a certain mean proportional and so to double the altar by it. And when they had done so they were at once rid of the plague. He discovered things in ethics too: not teaching for a fee, which belongs to ethics, he first …

… discovered. Indeed Pythagoras, and all before him, gave out his own teaching for a hundred drachmas of gold, being a retailer of words rather than a philosopher; and so Plato too bought the Timaeus [the book of Timaeus the Pythagorean] from the Pythagoreans for seven [the scan: 'seven of silver'] and wrote his dialogue in imitation of it; and so a verse of this sort is current: 'For much silver you got in exchange a little song; starting from it you set your hand to writing Timaeuses.' He discovered things in politics too: he was the first to find that the soldiers' arrangement [the scan: 'tēbadas'] should be circular, as holding more; for it has been shown by the geometers that of all figures with an equal perimeter the circle holds the most. He found also the third kind of constitution, the one based on a supposition. And he discovered things in theology, for example that the Ideas are in the paradigmatic cause; not that others before him did not know that they exist: Pythagoras said they were in the productive cause, and Aristotle after him [too] in the productive; but Plato himself, as has been said, said they were in the paradigmatic cause, which is beyond the productive. Indeed they say that when he had discovered the Ideas he saw himself with a third eye. He discovered also what eternity (aiōn) is. For those before him called the endlessness of time eternity; he showed that the endlessness of time is one thing and eternity another. He discovered also the dialogue as a form of writing; if anyone should say that Zeno and Parmenides wrote dialogues before him, we will reply that he used it most of all. 6. He lived 81 years, and by this too shows that he was Apollonian; for the number of the Muses, 9, multiplied by itself, produces the number 81; and that the Muses are handmaids of Apollo no one will deny. This number 81 is called a 'power of a power', since 3 is the first number because it has beginning, middle and end; 3 multiplied produces 9 (three times three is nine), and 9 produces the number 81. His divinity can also be learnt from what happened after his life. A woman went to ask the oracle whether she should place his statue among the statues of the gods; and the god answered thus: 'You would do well to honour Plato, the guide of godlike wisdom; a noble favour will repay you from the blessed ones, among whom that man is counted.' Another oracle was given, that two sons would be born, Asclepius to Apollo and Plato to Ariston, of whom one would be a healer of bodies, the other of souls. And the Athenians, celebrating his birthday, chant: 'On this day the gods gave Plato to men.' See also the superiority he had over Pythagoras: Pythagoras went off to Persia, wishing to profit from the wisdom of the Magi; but the Magi came to Athens because of Plato, longing to share in his philosophy. 7. Now that we have learnt the history of Plato, come, let us describe the character of his philosophy too. There have been many schools of philosophers before Plato and after Plato, and he outshot them all, in doctrines, in thought, in everything at once. Before him there were these schools: the poetic, whose leaders were Orpheus, Homer, Musaeus and Hesiod; there was also the one from the Ionian school, begun by Heraclitus, Thales and Anaxagoras; and there was that of Pythagoras and Parmenides. After Plato came the Stoic, the Epicurean, the Peripatetic and that of the New Academy. Those of the New Academy differ from the Sceptics (the 'suspenders of judgement') in this: the Sceptics say that [ungraspability] has spread through all things alike, the New Academy not through all alike, but that there are some things that move our soul, and a measured assent. Plato was seen to be better than all of these. From the poetic school he took the hymning of the order of the things that are; but he surpassed it, because the poets said everything without proof, and, as he himself says, 'with a raving and inspired mouth', while he said everything with proof. He surpassed them too in the seemliness of his myths. They wove their myths at random; he says that those who are going to weave a myth about god must keep certain rules, attending to which, and meeting with which, [readers] will not be deceived. For one must know that god is good and never puts forward falsehood, neither through ignorance of the truth nor through some deceitfulness; and that every god is unchangeable and unalterable: for he …

… changes neither for the worse nor for the better: the one is not in his nature, the other he cannot do; it is not in his nature to change for the worse, and he cannot change for the better, being himself better than all things. This is the seemliness of myths [Republic II 379a-383c]. Those who meet with a myth must keep this in mind, so that children are not wronged, but rather, through their attending at once to what is said, do not have to wait, as with Aesop's fables, for the moral, wishing to learn the use of the fable from it, but the good in it is clear to them at once. For children, if they do not attend to these things, will keep what they heard wrongly, hard to wash out. 8. So he surpassed the poets by being more demonstrative and more seemly. He surpassed also those from the Ionian school, who were natural philosophers. For one must know that they spoke of the contributory causes (synaitia); but he distinguished the causes from one another and said which are the causes: the paradigmatic, the productive, the final. And though Anaxagoras, as if dreaming out of a deep sleep, says that the productive cause is intellect, still he did not use it in coming-to-be and perishing, but blamed whirls of air and winds, nowhere making intellect the cause [Phaedo 98b-c]. Again, when they said that the elements are matter, he showed that they do not even hold the place of syllables: for he says that formless matter is like the 24 letters, body without qualities like the syllables, and the 4 elements like words; so that the elements do not even hold the place of syllables [Timaeus 48b-c]. So Plato rises above these too, and is more demonstrative than the first and more inspired than the second. From the Pythagoreans he took the signifying of things through numbers; indeed he used this way in the Timaeus. But he surpassed them too by being at once clearer and more demonstrative; for in the Timaeus itself he is seen to show things through numbers more clearly and [a word is unreadable in the scan]. He rose above the philosophy of Parmenides, because Parmenides said that the principle of the things that are is being (to on), while he showed that it is not, but that before it there is the One (to hen). For if being were the principle, all things would desire being, since all things depend on their own principle; but as it is we see some who despise existence for the sake of a greater good. So being is not the single principle of all things, but the One, which is beyond being.

9. So he took the first place among the philosophers before him, for the reasons given; and he rose above all those after him too. He was shown to be better than the Stoics, because they say that all things that are are bodies, while he showed that there are also incorporeal things. For he showed that the soul is incorporeal; and if it is incorporeal, then the angels before it will be incorporeal, and intellect, which is before them, and the first cause, which he calls the Good. He surpassed the Epicureans too. They said that the things here have no providence, and that the Demiurge's providence goes only as far as the heavenly bodies; for they say he would have trouble and would endure labours if he provided for these things too. But Plato showed that the things here also belong to providence; and he escaped the absurdities both of the first and of the second, and chose what is true in both. For the first, I mean the Stoics, who say that all things that are are bodies, an absurdity follows: that the Demiurge will need leverage and touch if he is to govern the things here; for bodies are acted upon through leverage, when the body acting upon them is another. This absurdity, which followed for them, he escaped by showing that there are some incorporeal things; and he chose [from them] that the divine provides for the things here. The absurdity that followed for the Epicureans, that the Demiurge does not provide for all things, Plato avoided too; for he does not say, as they do, that providence comes about through leverage: being incorporeal, he exercises such providence with no labour and no weariness. Besides what has been said, he had some advantage over the Peripatetics too. They thought that the principle of all things is intellect; he showed that before intellect there is the One, and before all the rest. For if intellect were the principle of the things that are, all things would think, since all things depend on their own principle; but as it is we see some things that do not think; so intellect is not the principle. [He surpassed them] also in that the Peripatetics say that intellect is the final cause of all things that are, while Plato showed that [the One] is the productive cause of the things that are, not [only] the final. We can show in another way too that intellect is not the first cause: if it were, since there are many Forms, there will be many intellects; and if so, the principle will be a multitude, which is absurd; for the principle must begin from one. 10. He surpassed also the philosophy of the New Academics …

… because it holds that nothing can be grasped (akatalēpsia), while he showed that there are some knowing graspings. Some, pushing Plato in with the Sceptics and the New Academics, say that he too brings in ungraspability, and they make their case from what he says in his writings. He uses, they say, ambiguous and doubtful adverbs when he discusses things, such as 'likely', 'perhaps', and 'probably, I think'; and this is not the mark of one who knows, but of one who has not grasped exact knowledge. To these we reply that he says these things by way of qualification, which the Sceptics do not do: they neither discuss precisely nor qualify, since they say that nothing at all can be grasped. Their second argument: from the fact that he argues for opposite things about the same subjects, it is plain that he holds ungraspability; for example, discussing friendship in the Lysis he argued for opposites, and about temperance in the Charmides, and about piety in the Euthyphro. To these we will say that even if he argued for opposites, in the end he decided where the truth lies. Third, they say that he does not think there is knowledge: this is clear because he refuted every account of knowledge, [and their number,] in the Theaetetus; how then shall we say that such a man holds that things can be grasped? To them we will say that Plato does not think the soul is like an unwritten tablet; he holds that it needs only uncovering, to sober up and see things; since it has knowledge within itself, but is dimmed by its joining with the body. So it needs only purification. That is why he refuted the accounts of knowledge that were badly stated, leaving the soul, once purified, to think the truth. A fourth argument of theirs is of this sort: if Plato thinks that knowing is twofold, one kind coming through the senses, the other through intellect, and says that each of them errs, it is plain that he holds ungraspability. For he says: 'we neither see nor hear anything exactly, but the senses go wrong' [Phaedo 65b]; and again about the things of intellect he says that our soul, entwined with this evil, the body, thinks nothing [Phaedo 66b]. To these we will say: when he says that the senses do not apprehend the things of sense, he means that they do not know the being of the things of sense; since of the affection produced in them by the things of sense themselves …

… that is produced they are aware, but they do not know the being itself, taken by themselves. For example, sight, being affected by white, perceives; but what white is it does not know by itself, but recognises it when joined with imagination; just as opinion too, by itself, does not know what it knows together with discursive thought (dianoia). Again, when he says that the soul does not think while it is with this evil [the body], he does not say this of all men, but of those who live in matter: for they have their soul overcome by the body; these he elsewhere calls 'sown men', springing up like plants; but the pure, whom he elsewhere calls citizens of heaven, these do think. The fifth argument is this: he himself, they say, says in one of his dialogues, 'I know nothing and teach nothing, I only raise difficulties'; see, then, how with his own mouth he admits that he has grasped nothing. To these too we say: when he says 'I know nothing', he is comparing his own knowledge with the knowledge of the gods; for that is other than ours: ours is bare knowledge only, while god's is effective in action; and theirs knows by a simple intuition, we through causes and premises. Again, he says 'I teach no one' in the sense 'I put my doctrines into no one'; for, as has been said, he does not liken the soul to an unwritten tablet, as if to write things into it when it does not have them; rather, as one bringing them to light and only reminding, he clears the soul, like those who wipe away the rheum that blocks the eyes. Indeed, as he says elsewhere, it is the one questioned who draws the conclusion; for this reason he gives [as answer] what seems right to him. 11. That raising difficulties is a road to grasping is plain to everyone. And besides, when he said 'I know nothing', he added 'except some small thing', and this is the taking and giving of an account, that is, conversing; so he knows dialectic. Again, elsewhere he says that he knows the things of love, as in other places midwifery; and through these three he is seen, in the Phaedrus, hymning the divine, calling it good and beautiful and wise. For as dialectic has gone through all the sciences, and all things desire the good, he said there that the good corresponds to dialectic, the beautiful to the art of love (for I love beautiful things), and the wise to midwifery. For as it is the work of the wise to bring to light what lies hidden in the depths of the soul and to [deliver] its birth-pangs [the end of the page is unreadable in the scan] …

… to bring out, so too it is the work of midwifery to bring out the child lying deep within. Since, then, we have written out their arguments in this way, come, let us show on its own account too that Plato was not of this opinion. For how could he be such a man who said and declared that he would boast of nothing so much as having escaped the method of division [as printed]? And again in the Gorgias he brings in Socrates speaking and making his partner in conversation agree to his questions; indeed he says: 'if you do not hear it from yourself, you will not be persuaded by another saying it'. How then shall we reckon such a man a Sceptic? 12. Since, then, we have learnt that his philosophy excels all others and that he is dogmatic and not sceptical, come, let us describe too the procession and order of the things that are, according to Plato. He said, then, that there is one principle of all things, not two as Empedocles said, nor infinitely many as the Epicureans; and that this principle is not a body, as the Stoics say, but incorporeal; and, being incorporeal, not life, for then all things would live, nor soul, nor intellect, nor being, because of the same absurdities; but the One, which he also calls the Good. After this, he says, there are the Limit and the Unlimited, and after these the intelligible cosmos; after this the gods above the cosmos; after these the gods within the cosmos; after these the 12 [the scan: 'eb'] kinds of angels; then the souls of men, and so those of the irrational animals; and next the soul of plants; and so body, material and immaterial, mortal and immortal; and the form in matter; and last of all, matter. 13. Since we have learnt Plato's history and the character of his philosophy, come, let us begin on the third heading too and discuss his writings. First let us resolve the difficulty raised because he thought his own doctrines worth writing down. For he himself, they say, in the Phaedrus finds fault with those who write, because writings, being soulless, cannot give an account to one who raises a difficulty, since they always say the same thing and cannot resolve a difficulty raised against them [Phaedrus 275d-e]; so one ought not, he says, to write, but to leave behind pupils, who are writings with souls. For those before him were accustomed to do this; and so Socrates and Pythagoras left behind only companions, not writings. That is the difficulty. We say [page 208 of the printing begins here] that in this too he imitated the divine when he thought fit to write, choosing a greater good in place of a lesser evil. For as the divine made some of the things it fashioned invisible, such as all the incorporeal things, angels and souls and intellects and the like, and others falling under our senses and visible, such as the heavenly bodies and the things in coming-to-be and perishing, so he too handed down some things in writing, and some without writing, not falling under the senses, like the incorporeal things: such are the things he said in his lectures; indeed Aristotle wrote about the unwritten lectures of Plato. So that in this too he might show his friendship towards the divine, he was eager to imitate it; for friends are eager to imitate one another. 14. So much on these matters. It is worth asking why he used the dialogue form. But before we learn the reason for this, let us say what a dialogue is. A dialogue, then, is speech without metre, composed of question and answer between various characters, with the portrayal of character proper to them. 'Without metre' is added because of the speech of comedy and tragedy, which is in metre: for it too is composed of question and answer between various characters with the portrayal of character it needs. It is worth asking why, when Plato elsewhere finds fault with variety in things (he finds fault with flute-playing because it uses varied instruments with many holes, with lyre-playing for its different strings, with comedy for the variety of its characters, and likewise with tragedy), why, finding fault with these for this reason, he himself has used this form of writing, the dialogue, composed of various characters. We must say that the variety of characters in the comic and tragic poets is not of the same sort as in Plato. In them, there being good and bad characters, the characters remain as they are; in Plato, even if one can find this too, good and bad characters I mean, one may see them changing: the bad being taught by the good, purified, and turning wholly away from the life of matter. So the variety in those poets is one thing and in him another; so he did not fall into contradiction.

15. We must, then, give the reasons why he used such a form of writing. We say, then, that he did this because the dialogue is a sort of cosmos. For as in the dialogue there are different characters, each speaking as befits him, so in the cosmos there are different natures uttering different voices; for each utters according to its own nature. Imitating, then, the divine works, the cosmos I mean, he did this too. Either for this reason, or because the cosmos is a dialogue. For as in the cosmos there are some natures higher and some lower, and the soul, abiding in it, now sides with the higher, now with the lower, so in the dialogue there are some characters who refute and some who are refuted, and our soul, being like a judge, gives itself now to those who refute, now to those refuted. Or [third] because, as Plato himself says, a speech is like a living creature [Phaedrus 264c]; then the most beautiful speech will correspond to the most beautiful of living creatures; and the most beautiful living creature is the cosmos; and the dialogue corresponds to it, as we said above; so the dialogue is the most beautiful speech. The fourth reason is this: since our soul delights in imitation, and the dialogue is an imitation of different characters, he did this so as to charm, as it were, our soul. That our soul delights in imitation is shown by our love of stories when we are children. Another reason after this is this: that he practised this form of writing so as not to hand down things to us bare and stripped of persons; for example, discussing friendship, so as not to speak of friendship bare but of friendship in such-and-such a man; and of ambition not by itself but of the ambition in such-and-such a man. For in this way our soul, seeing others refuted or praised, is more compelled to agree with the refutations or to emulate those praised. And this is like the souls in Hades that see others punished for their sins and grow temperate from fear of the punishments inflicted on them. Sixth, he practised the dialogue form so as to imitate dialectic: for as dialectic proceeds by question and answer, so the dialogue proceeds from characters questioned and answering; so that, as dialectic compels the soul to bring out the birth-pangs of the things it has in itself …

… (for the soul, in his view, is not like an unwritten tablet), and to agree with what is said, for the sake of this he used such a manner of writing. Seventh, so that we may attend to what is said because those speaking are different, and not, with one teacher always speaking, nod off, and suffer what the orator [Aeschines, as printed] suffered when he came forward, because he was one, the same man speaking from beginning to end. For he, being on the platform and speaking, because he did not converse, asking and being asked, did not rouse his hearers, but the jurors were borne off to sleep; seeing which the orator said to them: 'May you have had a good dream about the case!' Those who converse, then, are roused by asking and being asked. Indeed Alcibiades was so roused by the words of Socrates that he said of him: 'Socrates, my heart leaps at your words more than the Corybants', and I weep' [Symposium 215e]. For if [these words] lay hold of a well-endowed man, they hold on to him like a wild viper, hard to shake off [Symposium 217e-218a]. For all these reasons, then, he practised the dialogue form of expression. 16. Let us look into the fifth heading after those already discussed: how many are the things that make up each of Plato's dialogues. Since we have learnt that the dialogue is a cosmos and the cosmos a dialogue, we shall find in the dialogues as many components as make up the cosmos. In the whole cosmos there are matter, form, nature (which has put form into matter), soul, intellect and divinity. In the dialogue, matter corresponds to the characters, and the time and the place in which Plato wrote the dialogues [set them]. The characters one can find in every dialogue; but time and place we cannot name in every one, as in the Minos and the Cleitophon. And this is reasonable: for the matter in the proper sense is the characters, not the time and the place. As in things that come to be there must be matter, and if it is absent, since it is one of the causes, what comes to be does not come to be, while time and place hold the place of things 'without which not', so without characters there is no dialogue at all, since in defining the dialogue we said that it is composed of many characters asking and being asked. For this reason, then, we have the characters in plenty, but not always the time and the place. These characters are either …

… knowing, or holding right opinion, or ignorant; and the ignorant are ignorant with simple ignorance, or double, or the greatest, or the sophistic. Simple ignorance is when one does not know that something is so, and knows that he does not know. Double, when one both does not know that something is so and does not know that he does not know, as he says in the Phaedrus: 'I cannot yet, as the Delphic inscription bids, know myself' [as printed; Phaedrus 229e]. The greatest ignorance is when one both does not know and knows that he does not know, but, held by the passion for the opposite doctrine, does not leave his own ignorance. Sophistic ignorance is when one does not know, but hastens to cover his ignorance with plausible talk. These characters are neither wholly historical (for Plato could not have recorded even the smallest things, such as that Socrates bent his leg), nor is everything about the characters invented (for then they would not have the truth); but Plato says the things that tend to the proof of one matter, like painters who pick out the colours suited to painting one form. So much about the characters. As to time, he published his dialogues not at any time, but when there were festivals and feasts of the gods, so that his writings might then be hymned and proclaimed like hymns; for at feasts we are accustomed to recite hymns. Indeed the Timaeus he published at the Bendideia (this is a festival of Artemis in the Piraeus), the Parmenides at the Panathenaea, and others at other feasts. So much about the time. As to place, he brings in different places in his dialogues at different times. While Socrates was alive he set the scenes of the dialogues in Athens; after he died, no longer in Athens, because he thought the Athenians unworthy of his words [as printed]. Indeed the Symposium he worked out in Agathon's house, the Republic in the Piraeus, the Phaedrus at the shrine of the Nymphs, the Timaeus not in some particular place but in the city; and others in other places. So much about the place. 17. These, then, correspond to matter. To form corresponds the style. It is either grand, or plain, or mixed; and if mixed, either by blending or by juxtaposition. He used the grand style in the theological dialogues, the plain in the other dialogues, imitating in his diction the things [he speaks of] …

[… before] we learn in which [dialogues] he used the style mixed by blending, let us first say what the style mixed by blending is, and of what sort. We say, then, that the grand style toned down, or the plain style that has a little grandeur, is mixed by blending; mixed by juxtaposition, when part of the dialogue is expressed plainly and part grandly, as he does in the Gorgias: what comes before the myth is expressed plainly, what is in the myth grandly, for the reason just given, that he expresses theological matters grandly and logical matters plainly. The style mixed by blending he used in the ethical dialogues, since in them he discusses virtue, and the virtues are means; and the style mixed by blending is, in the proper sense, a mean. The manner of the conversation corresponds to nature. It is either expository, or inquiring, or mixed: it is expository when he puts forward his own views without any inquiry or proof; inquiring when he inquires; mixed when it is made of both. Each of the extremes is divided in two: of the expository, one is theoretical, the other political; and of the inquiring, one is competitive, the other for exercise. He used the theoretical expository manner in the theological dialogues, and the political expository manner in the Republics. To soul correspond the proofs, for soul puts the proofs forward; to intellect, the problem, about which the proofs are put forward like a circumference. And reasonably the problem is like intellect: for as intellect is without parts and is thought of like a centre, and the objects of discursive thought are about intellect like a circumference unrolling about the centre, so too is the problem, and the proofs unroll about it like a circumference, wishing to hunt down the problem set. [To divinity corresponds] the good. So much has been said thus. It can be shown in another way too how the things that make up the dialogue correspond to those in the cosmos. Since there are six causes for each thing that comes to be, the material, the formal, the productive, the final, the paradigmatic and the instrumental: to the material correspond the characters, the time and the place; to the formal the style; to the productive the soul; to the instrumental the proofs; to the paradigmatic the problems; to the final the good. 18. The sixth heading we must look into is where Plato takes the titles of his dialogues from. We say, then, that [he takes them] from …

… persons or from things; and from persons, either those who bring to completion, or those who are brought to completion, or those who perform some service. From those who bring to completion, as he did with the Parmenides and the Timaeus; from those brought to completion, as with the Alcibiades and the Phaedrus and the like; from those performing some service, as with the Crito. If he takes the titles from things, he takes them either from what happened, as with the Apology, for this is about what happened; or from what is inquired into, as with the Sophist; or from the … [a gap in the printed text]. 19. Let the seventh heading after those discussed be set before us for inquiry: to learn from what one should find the divisions into sections of each dialogue. Since each dialogue has three things, story and characters, dialectic and syllogisms, and doctrines, one should not make the divisions from the story and the characters, as some do, dividing the Gorgias into the conversations with Gorgias, Polus and Callicles; one should not make them from these, for often, arguing about some matter, he is accustomed to give part of the argument to the second story and the second character. Nor should one make the divisions from the dialectic and the syllogisms, as some do, dividing the Alcibiades into the ten syllogisms handed down in it; not from these either, for the same reason: for often he gives different syllogisms about the same matter, so that the proof is not completed in one syllogism. One must make the divisions from the doctrines. 20. [The eighth heading after those discussed we must look into: what kind of manner of conversation the characters in the dialogue have. One must know, then, that he holds the conversation either through the characters themselves, as when he brings in Socrates himself, or some other, conversing in his own person; or through some others who heard it from the characters, as when he brings in someone discussing matters he heard from Socrates; or through others, of those who learnt it from those who heard Socrates; or through others who heard it from the second hearers; so that the series of hearers goes as far as these and proceeds no further. In this too he is seen imitating the order of the things that are. For he does not go beyond the third, since all the things that are are either intelligible …

… or objects of discursive thought, which are images of the intelligibles; or sensible, which are themselves images of the objects of discursive thought; or images of the sensibles, such as those made by painters; and beyond these there is nothing, so that here too there are four. The characters correspond to the intelligibles; those who heard from them to the objects of discursive thought, for they are like images of the characters themselves, as the objects of discursive thought are of the intelligibles; and the second hearers correspond to the sensibles. 21. The ninth heading after those discussed we must look into: by how many rules one must hunt for the aim (skopos) of each dialogue. There is need to look for it since, as he himself says in the Phaedrus, 'My boy, there is one beginning for those who mean to deliberate well: to know what the deliberation is about; or else one must miss the whole' [Phaedrus 237b-c]. How then, when he himself says this, shall we excuse ourselves, with his own writings, from knowing what each of them discusses? We would learn the usefulness of such an inquiry still more if we attended to the double titles of most of the dialogues. For almost every one has a double title, such as 'Phaedo, or On the Soul', and 'Phaedrus, or On Beauty', and the others likewise; so it is unclear which of the things contained in the title it discusses; so we do not look into this heading uselessly. One can hunt the aim from ten headings: from the one and the many; from the universal and the particular; from the whole and the part; from the broad and the precise; from the better and the worse; from what agrees and what does not; from its not being said against someone; from its not being full of passion; from the instruments; from the matter. From the one and the many: so that we say that the dialogue has one aim and not many. For how could a dialogue of Plato's have many aims, when he so hymns the divine, which is one? And in another way: if he himself is the one who says that a dialogue is like a living creature, since a speech is (for every speech well written corresponds to a living creature [Phaedrus 264c]); if, then, the dialogue corresponds to a living creature, and the living creature has one end, the good, for the sake of which it came to be, then the dialogue too must have one end, that is, one aim. Hence we must not accept those who say that the Phaedo has three aims, the immortality of the soul, a good death, and the philosophic life; they speak badly, as has been said [page 215 of the printing begins here]; for the aims must not be many, but one. From the universal and the particular: so that we choose the more universal and more inclusive aim rather than the more particular. Hence we must not accept those who say that the Sophist has as its aim the sophist, but accept those who say it is about not-being: for the sophist is a particular not-being, and not-being simply is more universal than a particular not-being; and if more universal, then more inclusive too; so the more universal aim includes the particular. From this it is clear (it emerges for us as a sort of corollary) that the titles of the dialogues should not be double: for either they are different from each other, or one and the same, or one more universal and the other more particular. If, then, they are different, we will not accept them, so as not to choose many aims and so fall into the absurdities of the first rule; if one and the same, the second was taken in vain, as idle talk; if the second is more universal, the universal one must be chosen. 22. From the whole and the part: so that we do not take the aim from what is said in some short part of the dialogue, but from what is taught in the whole. So we find fault with those who say the Phaedrus has rhetoric as its aim: for it discusses rhetoric there for a little while, but in the whole dialogue it treats of beauty of every kind; so one must say that the aim is about that. And again we find fault with those who say that in the Gorgias Plato's aim is to discuss whether it is better to do wrong or to be wronged: for he teaches about this in a small part, but in the whole dialogue about the ethical principles of happiness. For as those do badly who say that man came to be for the sake of some one of the parts in man, such as seeing or hearing or some other such thing (for he did not come to be for this, but in order to be a mean between the divine and the things that come to be; for he is neither immortal like the divine, nor mortal like the irrational, but shares in some respect in both), so we find fault with those who take the aim from a part. And in another way: if Plato imitates nature everywhere, how will he not imitate nature in this too? For if the part corresponds to matter and the whole to form, and nature makes form, and this is its aim, to put form in, how should he not, putting in …

… a sort of form, imitate the whole in his aim and not take it from the part? From the broad and the precise: so that we choose the precise aim rather than the broad and remote. Here too, then, we will not accept those who say that the aim of the Timaeus is to teach about natural philosophy: for this is broad and remote; for Aristotle too teaches about natural philosophy, and many others, and it is unclear what natural philosophy it discusses, if we attend only to this aim and to the title of the dialogue. We must, then, moving more precisely, say that the aim is about natural philosophy according to Plato, and what natural philosophy according to Plato is, and not simply about natural philosophy. From the better and the worse: so that we choose the better aim rather than the worse. So we do not accept those who say that the aim in the Gorgias is to refute the rhetoric of Polus and Gorgias: for this is shameful and sophistic; rather, the dialogue sets out to teach true rhetoric, which is better and wonderful. If someone should say, 'Why then does he mention Polus and Gorgias, bringing them in as partners in the conversation and refuting what they say?', we will say that, just as nature has as its aim to put form into matter, not to remove privation, but the removal of privation follows on the putting in of form, so too on the arguments that show true rhetoric there follows the refutation of the rhetoric of Polus and Gorgias. From what agrees and what does not: so that we choose the aim that agrees with what is said rather than those that do not. Using this rule we will refute those who say that the Gorgias has as its aim the intellect that sees itself: for this disagrees with, and is wholly out of tune with, what is taught there. Nor must one say that the aim of the dialogue is against someone: for the divine Plato is not such as to choose to attack. So we will refute those who say that the aim of the Menexenus is to attack and compete with Thucydides: for the funeral speech, they say, was written by him for this, wishing to write a reply to Thucydides' funeral speech; which is false. 23. From what is not full of passion: the aim must not be full of passion, so that it does not put a passion in the readers …

… to look down to matter; as some do badly who say that the Philebus has pleasure as its aim, which can drag the soul down; for how could one belonging to a purificatory life discuss pleasure? So his aim is not about this, but about the order of the six goods. From the instruments: so that we do not take the aim from these; for the aim is not that by means of which, but that for the sake of which. So those do badly who say that the Sophist has as its aim the art of division; for he mentions it there; indeed he says there that he will boast of nothing so much as having escaped [as printed] the power of division; for he says this division is a gift to men from the gods through Prometheus [Philebus 16c]. Since, then, it is an instrument of demonstration and is among the things that contribute to the aim (for we use it in order to hunt the aim), one must not take the aim from it. One must not take it from the matter, as some do, saying that the Alcibiades has as its aim the ambition of Alcibiades: they speak badly, taking the aim from the matter; for one must not do this; and by the matter of the dialogues we mean the characters. For his aim is not to refute the ambition in Alcibiades' soul, since we would fall into the absurdity of the second rule, bringing in the particular in place of the universal. It is better, then, to say universally that the aim is to refute the ambition in every soul; for in each of us there is a sort of Alcibiadean ambition, which must be brought into rhythm and order for the better. Nor is it fitting to say that the divine Plato lowered himself to such things as refuting the passions of men; though refutation does wholly follow upon his arguments. From so many [rules], then, one must hunt the aim of each dialogue. 24. Let the tenth heading be to learn the order of Plato's dialogues. Some have said that their order should be taken from time and from the tetralogy; and from time in two ways: either from the time of Plato, or from the time of the characters in the dialogues. From the time of the writer, they say that the Phaedrus is first, since in it, they say, he inquires whether one ought to write or not; but how could he, when he is in doubt there whether one ought to write, have written another before it? And besides, because in it he used the dithyrambic …

… style, as if he had not yet put off the muse of the dithyrambs. They say the Laws were written last, because he left them uncorrected and in disorder, not having had the time, because of his death, to put them together; and if they now seem to be arranged as they should be, it was not Plato himself who put them together but one Philip of Opus, who became a successor in Plato's school. From the time of the characters in them: on this view they say the Parmenides is first, because it supposes Socrates very young, being taught by Parmenides, and the Theaetetus last, because it is set after the death of Socrates [as printed]. From the tetralogies: on this view they say that he published the dialogues in tetralogies, in imitation of the tragic and comic poets, who competed with four plays having the same aim, and in the last came round to pleasure. 25. They say, then, that there are nine tetralogies, so that all his dialogues number 36; and these people, so that the number of the tetralogies may stand, declare the Epinomis, which is held spurious, to be genuine. That it is spurious the most wise Proclus shows by two arguments: first, asking how a man who did not manage to correct the Laws, because he did not have the time of life, could have written the Epinomis after them; second, that in his other dialogues he says that the planets move from right to left, but in this one the reverse, from left to right. Those who say the dialogues were published in tetralogies say that the first tetralogy is the Euthyphro, the Apology, the Crito and the Phaedo. They say the Euthyphro comes first, since in it Socrates is supposed as about to be tried; second the Apology, since in it he is on trial; third the Crito, since in it Socrates has already been tried; fourth the Phaedo, since in it he dies. Last of all, they say, the Letters were written; they think the Euthyphro first because in the Euthyphro he discusses much about the life of Socrates, and in the Letters he goes through much about his own life; so that, to begin and end with the same thing, he used such an order. We will not accept them when they say …

… that he practised the tetralogy form in imitation of the tragic poets: for he himself finds fault with them, saying that they write images of images [Republic X 596-598]. And it can be shown another way that he does not imitate them: they come round to pleasure at the last, but he, in the Phaedo, the last of the first tetralogy, did not come round to pleasure but to the death of Socrates. So they are wrong to say that his dialogues were published in tetralogies. And besides, the aim of the Euthyphro is one thing, of the Apology another, of the Crito another, of the Phaedo another. 26. To learn the true order, let us first say which are the spurious dialogues, and not look for an order for these. Everyone agrees, then, that the Sisyphus, the Demodocus, the Halcyon, the Eryxias and the Definitions are spurious, which they ascribe to Speusippus [the scan has a gap: '…rous'; the Definitions]; so that all [the genuine] are 36, of which the divine Proclus rejects the Epinomis as spurious, for the reasons given. He [Proclus] leaves out the Republic too, because it is many books and not written as a dialogue, and the Laws for the same reason; and he leaves out the Letters because of their simple style; so that 32 dialogues in all remain; and when the 12 books of the Laws and the 10 of the Republic are added to these, all the dialogues number 54. The order of all these, as not very useful and too long for a short account, we pass over; we shall say what the divine Iamblichus did. He divided the whole into twelve dialogues, and of these called some physical and some theological; and again he gathered the twelve into two, the Timaeus and the Parmenides, the Timaeus over all the physical, the Parmenides over the theological. Of these it is worth looking into the order, because everyone has thought fit to study these. First, then, one must study the Alcibiades, because in it we come to know ourselves; and it is fitting to know ourselves before knowing what is outside us: for how can we know those things if we are ignorant of ourselves? And last must come the Philebus, since in it he discusses the Good, which is beyond all things; so it too must be beyond all and last. Those in the middle must be ordered thus. Since the virtues are five in rank, by depth: natural, ethical …

… political, purificatory, contemplative: first [of the middle dialogues] one must read the Gorgias, as being political; second, the Phaedo, as purificatory (for after the political life comes the purifying); then we come to the knowledge of the things that are, which comes about through ethical virtue. These things that are are contemplated either in concepts or in things; so after the dialogues named one must read, fourth, the Cratylus, as teaching about names, then the Theaetetus, as being about things. Then after these we come to the one teaching about natural things [a dialogue seems to have dropped out of the text here; see the Workshop's note in the reading order], and so on to the Phaedrus and the Symposium, as discussing theological matters in a contemplative way; and so one must come to the perfect dialogues, I mean the Timaeus and the Parmenides. So we speak about these. But since some think the Laws and the Republic should be studied as well, it is worth stating their aim too. There are three kinds of constitution: the one by correction, the one by supposition, and the one without supposition. By correction, when we make the bad habits of our own soul straight; by supposition, when they lay down laws and certain customs in cities; without supposition, when nothing is laid down, but all things are common, so that 'mine' is here and 'yours' [the scan has a gap], and each man's property is both his own and another's. About the one by correction he treats in the Letters, about the one by supposition in the Laws, and about the one without supposition in the Republic. 27. The last heading to look into, among the preliminaries to Plato's dialogues, is to know what manner of teaching Plato uses. He uses fifteen manners of teaching: the inspired, the demonstrative, the defining, the dividing, the analytic, the evidential, the one by images, the one by examples, the inductive, the analogical, the numerical, the one by subtraction, the one by addition, the historical, the etymological. The inspired he uses in the Phaedrus, when he is possessed by the Nymphs, and in the eighth [book] of the Republic, discussing the Muses, and in the Timaeus, acting the part of the Demiurge speaking to the heavenly gods, and in some others too. The demonstrative, in the Phaedo [as printed], showing the …

… immortality of the soul by means of the self-moving. The defining, in almost all the dialogues, both defining himself and getting his partners in conversation to define. The dividing he uses in the Sophist, saying, as we said above, that he will boast of nothing so much as having escaped [as printed] the method of division, given to men by god through Prometheus. The analytic he uses in the Timaeus, resolving all natural things into the receptacle and form (calling matter the receptacle), and form again into figures, and the figures into triangles, and saying that what lies beyond these only god knows, and the man who is dear to him [Timaeus 53d]. The evidential he uses in the Alcibiades, saying that disagreement is a sign of falsehood and agreement of truth; for the truth neither disagrees with itself nor fights itself. The one by images he uses in the Phaedrus, likening our soul to a charioteer and its powers to horses, calling one good and the other bad. The one by examples, in the Republic, saying that the city is like a ship, the people like the shipowner, and the rulers like sailors who want to make the shipowner drunk, so that they may have the power to do whatever they like [Republic VI 488]. The one by images differs from the one by examples in that the image shows and imitates more the nature of which it is an image, and the example imitates it less. Indeed one can call the true thing by the name of the image: if we call the soul a charioteer we would not be wrong; but by the name of the example one cannot: for who will call a city a ship? The cause of this is the greater or lesser likeness. The inductive he uses in the Alcibiades, where he says that one who persuades one can persuade many, and one who persuades many can persuade one; and this he establishes by induction: the geometer who persuades one can persuade many, and the same man persuading many can clearly persuade one. The analogical he uses in the Gorgias, saying that as medicine is to cookery, so justice is to sophistry. For as medicine, looking to the good and the beneficial, prescribes this remedy or this food even if it is unpleasant, while cookery looks only to the pleasant, seasoned with varied flavours, so justice does only what is beneficial and good, while rhetoric does what is pleasant …

… and there he calls rhetoric 'sophistry' [as printed]. Hence they say that Aeschines once went up onto the platform and said to his hearers: 'What do you want? What shall I say? How shall I please you?' What was said has been shown by geometrical proportion, as this to this. The numerical he uses in the Philebus, saying that there are six ranks of goods, and which they are, counting them off. The one by subtraction he uses in the Timaeus, keeping hold of and finding matter by the subtraction of all the forms. The one by addition, in the Alcibiades: he sets out to inquire what man is, whether body or soul or the two together; and shows that it is neither the body nor the two together, but the soul by itself; then going on he adds that it is not every soul, for not the vegetative or the irrational, but the rational; and again that man is a mean between the divine and the things that come to be; and see how, going on, he added to the inquiry. The historical he uses in the Laws, recounting events from the flood to the Persian wars; the etymological in the Theaetetus [as printed]. 28. Up to this point, then, let the preliminaries to the joint reading of Plato's philosophy be, gathered in eleven headings: one containing the history of the philosopher; another the character of his philosophy; a third why he came to write; a fourth why he practised the dialogue form of writing; a fifth what makes up the dialogues; a sixth from what the divisions of Plato's dialogues are to be made; a seventh from what the titles must be hunted; an eighth what manner of exposition he uses in the dialogues, that is, what the arrangement is; a ninth from what the aims of the dialogues are to be hunted; a tenth what the order of the dialogues is; and the last, in how many manners of teaching the most divine Plato teaches. [The scholia on the Euthyphro begin here in the printing.]
